text: I used to think shipping fast was about typing fast. It's not. It's about having fewer things to decide.
The hardest part of writing is not writing. It's deciding what the thing is actually about.
Every time I skip the outline, I end up rewriting the whole thing twice.
Nobody tells you that most of debugging is just reading your own code slowly.
I'd push back on that a little. Small teams aren't faster because they're small. They're faster because they argue less.
Turns out the bug was in the code I wrote to find the bug.
I don't think tools make you productive. I think they make you feel productive, which is not the same thing.
If you're rewriting it for the third time, the problem probably isn't the code.
I'll take a boring codebase over a clever one any day.
The thing about deadlines is they don't make you work faster. They make you cut things. Which is fine, as long as you know what you're cutting.
I spent four hours on a problem that a five minute conversation would have solved.
Most of my best decisions looked boring at the time.
Writing things down isn't about remembering them. It's about finding out whether they make sense.
I keep learning the same lesson: if it's hard to explain, I don't understand it yet.
Reading code is a skill. We just never practice it on purpose.
This is exactly it.
